summary: Describes LISP, an experimental network-layer protocol that separates IP addresses into Endpoint Identifiers and Routing Locators. It requires no changes to host stacks or the Internet core and can be deployed gradually. It was replaced by RFC 9300 and RFC 9301.

plainLanguage.summary: LISP separates two jobs that an IP address normally does together. A host still uses one address to name another host, but the address on the outer packet, which the routers in the network actually follow, is a different one belonging to a router at the edge of the site. The mapping between the two is looked up as needed, so hosts and the network core never have to agree.

subtitle: Splitting the IP address into an identity for hosts and an address for the network core.

tldr.problem: An IP address does two jobs at once: it tells a host who it is talking to, and it tells the routers in the network where to send the packet. That forces every site to advertise its own prefix to the whole Internet, which does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: LISP keeps the host address as an Endpoint Identifier and uses a separate, topologically assigned Routing Locator for the outer header. Routers at the edge look up the mapping between the two, put the LISP header on the packet, and the router at the far end takes it off again.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6830 is an Experimental document from January 2013 and has been obsoleted by RFC 9300 and RFC 9301, which restate the protocol.

today: RFC 6830 is an Experimental document from January 2013, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 9300 and RFC 9301, which restate the protocol; the unit metadata also lists RFC 8113 as updating it. The RFC notes that the document is published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation, and that design and development were largely motivated by the problem statement produced by the October 2006 IAB Routing and Addressing Workshop.

sections.title: Why Separate Identity from Location
sections.content:
Today an IP address does two jobs at once. It says which host a packet is for, and it says where in the network the packet should be routed. A site with two Internet connections has to advertise its own address block to the whole Internet so that traffic for either connection reaches it, and each such block has to be globally unique.

LISP splits those jobs. Hosts keep using addresses exactly as they do now, and those addresses are called Endpoint Identifiers. The addresses the routers in the network core follow are different, and are called Routing Locators; they belong to the tunnel routers at the edge of a site and come from ordinary, topologically aggregatable provider address space. A lookup between the two tells a router which locator to use to reach a given endpoint.

The RFC makes a point of how little changes. Host protocol stacks are untouched, and so is the core of the Internet. A host sends its packet as it always would, and a LISP router in the path intercepts the packet and encapsulates it. LISP can be deployed incrementally, without a flag day, and even a small number of LISP-capable sites can get traffic engineering, multihoming and mobility benefits.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem with IP addresses is that the name of a host and the instructions to the routers are the same string. LISP keeps the name for the host and issues a second, separate address for the routers to follow, so a site no longer needs its own globally unique block.

sections.title: EIDs, RLOCs and the Mapping Between Them
sections.content:
An EID is a 32-bit or 128-bit value used as the source and destination address in the innermost header of a packet. A host obtains a destination EID the same way it obtains a destination address today, for example through a DNS lookup. An EID is allocated to a host from an EID-Prefix block, a power-of-two block of EIDs handed to a site by an address allocation authority, and it must be globally unique to be usable on the public Internet. EIDs must never be used as RLOCs.

An RLOC is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of an Egress Tunnel Router. It is the result of a mapping lookup: an EID maps to one or more RLOCs. RLOCs come from topologically aggregatable blocks assigned to a site at each point where it attaches to the Internet, and several RLOCs can belong to one router or to several routers at a site. Because RLOCs are ordinary provider-assigned addresses, they aggregate into the provider's larger block and need no separate global announcement per site.

The mapping itself is stored in a distributed global database, and each router that serves as an egress tunnel router holds the part of it that concerns its own site. Separately, an ingress tunnel router keeps a small, short-lived cache of the mappings it has looked up, which is different from the database in that it is local, on-demand and quickly timed out.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of address and one table that connects them. The table is distributed: every egress router holds the entries for its own site, and the routers that need an entry look it up and keep it for a while in a small cache.

sections.title: How a Packet Travels Through LISP
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a concrete example. A source host resolves the destination name with DNS and gets an address, which is the destination EID; the host's own address is the source EID. The packet is built and forwarded as an ordinary IP packet through the site until it reaches an ingress tunnel router.

The ingress tunnel router cannot route an EID across the Internet, so it sends a Map-Request for the destination EID. Map-Requests should be rate-limited. The request may travel over the underlying routing system or over an alternative logical topology to a mapping system; either way it reaches one of the egress tunnel routers at the destination site. That router matches the destination EID against the prefixes in its own mapping database, drops the request if there is no match, and otherwise returns a Map-Reply.

The ingress router parses the reply, checks its format, and stores the mapping in its cache. Every later packet for that destination gets a LISP header prepended, with the learned locator as the outer destination address. The packet may go to a different egress router than the one that answered, because the source site hashes its traffic and the destination site has its own policy for choosing among its locators. The egress router receives the packet because the outer address is one of its own, checks the addresses, strips the header and forwards the packet to the destination host.
sections.plainLanguage: On the first packet, the edge router asks a question: what address should I put on the outside of this packet? The answer comes back as a Map-Reply and is remembered. Later packets are wrapped straight away using that answer, and the router at the far end takes the wrapper off before delivering the packet.

sections.title: The LISP Encapsulation
sections.content:
A LISP-encapsulated packet has an outer IP header, a UDP header, a LISP header and the original inner IP header with the packet's payload. The outer header's address fields hold the RLOCs; the inner header's hold the EIDs. The outer header uses protocol number 17 for UDP, and the UDP destination port must be the assigned value 4341. The UDP checksum should be sent as zero by the ingress router, and the egress router must accept a packet with a zero checksum and may choose not to verify a non-zero one.

The LISP header itself is two 32-bit words. The first carries five flag bits and a 24-bit field that holds either a nonce or a map version. The N bit says a nonce is present, and the nonce is a random value generated by the ingress router to prove that a Map-Reply answers a request that was actually made. The L bit says the second word is in use as locator status bits, the E bit asks for the nonce to be echoed back, the V bit says a map version is present, and the I bit says the high-order 24 bits of the second word carry an instance ID instead.

Adding headers makes packets larger, so the RFC recommends that IPv4 packets are not fragmented while being encapsulated, and that the packet is dropped and an ICMP Too Big message returned instead. Implementations are asked to support one of two fragmentation and reassembly schemes. All four combinations of IPv4 and IPv6 in the inner and outer headers must be supported, and a maximum of two LISP headers may be prepended to a packet, which is enough for one for location and identity separation at a site and one inside a provider for traffic engineering.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapped packet has two address headers. The inner one is the original, unchanged. The outer one carries the network address that the routers follow. Between them sits a small header with flags, a random value and status bits.

sections.title: The Mapping Messages
sections.content:
The control messages have their own simple format, sent over UDP. A Map-Request starts with a type field of 1, a set of flag bits, a five-bit count of the ingress router's own RLOCs, and a record count. It then carries a 64-bit nonce, the source EID, one or more ingress RLOC addresses, and one or more records, each of which holds a mask length, an address family and the EID prefix being asked about. The RFC says a sender must only send one record per request, though a receiver must accept more.

The flag bits say what kind of request it is. The authoritative bit distinguishes a request sent to the mapping database from one sent to the destination site asking it to answer. The map-data-present bit says a reply record is included in the request. The probe bit turns the request into a reachability probe for a locator. The solicit bit asks the recipient to refresh its own mappings, and the proxy bit marks a request from a proxy ingress router.

A Map-Reply carries the nonce back and a list of locator records, each with a priority, a weight, a reachability bit, a local bit and an address. When a UDP Map-Reply is sent the source port is 4342. A requester checks the nonce against the one it sent, which is what stops an off-path attacker from feeding it a false answer.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two control messages. The request asks for the addresses that belong to one block of endpoint identifiers, and the reply lists them with a priority and a weight so the requester can spread traffic across several of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most of the security is expected to come from the mapping database service. For mappings triggered by data traffic, the protection against a spoofed egress router comes from route returnability: a 24-bit nonce in the encapsulation header and a 64-bit nonce in the control message. An ingress router accepts only solicited Map-Replies, so it will only take an answer that carries the nonce it sent. It is hard for an off-path attacker to guess the nonce, and trying many values would already be a denial of service in itself. An on-path attacker can do much more, but it can already eavesdrop on, block or redirect traffic in the current Internet.

The RFC says LISP deliberately does not rely on a public key infrastructure or a heavier authentication system, because those would challenge the main design goal of scalability. Denial of service protection depends on rate-limiting Map-Requests and Map-Replies, and on rate-limiting the number of data-triggered Map-Replies.

Two further risks are named. An ingress router might ignore the priorities and weights in a Map-Reply, which lets a site steer its own traffic unevenly towards an egress router, no worse than a bandwidth attack the site could mount anyway. And an egress router can claim a shorter EID-Prefix than it is really responsible for, so mechanisms to detect that are left for future work. The section also warns about map-cache exhaustion, which is why a cap on cache entries with a reserve for frequently used sites is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The main defence is a random value that the requester chooses and only accepts back from the router it asked. That makes it hard for someone who is not on the path to feed a false answer. LISP deliberately avoids certificates, because they would not scale.

fields.name: N, L, E, V, I and flags
fields.desc: N says a nonce is present, L that locator status bits are in use, E that a nonce echo is requested, V that a map version is present, I that an instance ID is present. Three flag bits are reserved for future use.

fields.name: Nonce / Map-Version
fields.desc: A random value generated by the ingress tunnel router when the N bit is set, used to check that a Map-Reply answers a request that was made.

fields.name: Instance ID / Locator-Status-Bits
fields.desc: When the I bit is set the high-order 24 bits carry the instance ID and the low-order 8 bits the locator status bits. Otherwise the whole field carries locator status bits.
